title: Why LLMs in healthcare?
text:
Key Takeaways




LLMs excel at language tasks: summarising, drafting, translating, extracting, and answering questions with citations.
Use retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) to ground outputs in trusted local guidelines, pathways, and formularies.
Apply human‑in‑the‑loop review for all clinical outputs; LLMs can be helpful but are fallible.
Prioritise data privacy, governance, and prompt hygiene when handling sensitive information.




Administrative Tasks

AI Scribes (LLM-powered): Convert ambient consultation audio into structured draft notes (history, exam, plan) and generate draft discharge summaries or clinic letters. This can save 5-10 minutes per patient appointment.
Summarisation & Standardisation: Turn lengthy free-text notes into succinct summaries; convert variable discharge letters into standard templates with required fields; translate patient correspondence into plain language or other languages.
Information Extraction: Pull key entities (medications, allergies, dates, diagnoses) from unstructured clinical text for registry updates, handover lists, or quality improvement audits.



Clinical Decision Support

Guideline Q&A with Citations (RAG): Ask questions against trusted sources (local pathways, formulary, NICE/BNF, institutional policies) and receive grounded answers with direct links to source passages.
Chart Summarisation & Timeline Reconstruction: Condense years of notes into problem-oriented summaries; surface relevant history, medication changes, and key investigations to aid clinical decision-making during reviews or handovers.
Differential & Plan Drafting (for review): Generate candidate differential diagnoses, red flags, and draft management plans that must be checked by the clinician against current guidelines and individual patient context.







Human-in-the-Loop Principle



All LLM-generated clinical documentation must be reviewed, verified, and signed by the responsible clinician. You remain professionally and legally accountable for clinical records. Human review is essential to mitigate hallucinations, misinterpretations, and negligence risks.




Research and Innovation: Accelerating Evidence Work

Literature Triage & Summarisation: Screen abstracts against inclusion criteria; create structured summaries (PICO framework) from papers; accelerate systematic review processes.
Protocol & Document Drafting: Produce first drafts of study protocols, ethics applications.



Operational Efficiency: Improving Service Delivery

Policy & SOP Q&A (RAG): Enable staff to query institutional policies, safeguarding procedures, and escalation pathways.
Patient Education Materials: Generate patient-specific educational leaflets and discharge instructions in accessible language.

title: Context matters
text:
Key Takeaways




Context is all the information you give LLMs to understand your request (role, purpose, audience, requirements)
Be specific, not vague - Clear context gets relevant responses; vague prompts get generic ones
Refine iteratively - Start basic, review output, add details, repeat until satisfied
Never share sensitive data - No personal records, unpublished research, or confidential information



Large Language Models work by navigating through vast embedding spaces—multidimensional representations of knowledge and concepts. Vague or poorly defined context can lead the model to explore irrelevant areas of this space, producing generic or off-target responses. Well-crafted context act as precise navigation instructions, guiding the model to the most relevant knowledge areas and ensuring outputs that match your specific needs and context.



Multidimensional embedding space example.



Why Context Matters for LLMs
Context is everything you provide to an LLM to help it understand your request and generate appropriate responses during your chatbot session. Without proper context, LLMs often produce generic, inaccurate, or inappropriate outputs.
Because LLMs have no memory between separate sessions, they have no inherent knowledge about who you are, your organization’s policies or the purpose of your request.
Example of poor context

Write me a report about productivity

Example of better context

I am a manager at the North Bristol NHS Trust. I have to write a 2-page executive summary about remote work productivity for the Senior Management Team, focusing on evidence-based strategies and including practical implementation steps.”

Note that while LLMs have no memory between separate chat sessions and don’t retain information from previous conversations, the data you share within each individual session may still be stored by the service provider. Always follow University’s data protection policies when sharing any information.






AI Policy at NBT & UHBW (HG-IG-001)



Independently of the prompting framework you are using, never share these with unapproved or general-purpose AI tools:
🚫 Personal Identifiable Data (PID): Patient medical records, health status, NHS numbers, or staff personal files.
🚫 Sensitive Clinical Information: Diagnostic scans, consultation transcripts (from AI Scribes), or unverified discharge summaries.
🚫 Confidential Medical Research: Unpublished clinical trial findings, grant applications under review, or proprietary drug discovery data.
🚫 Commercially Sensitive Data: Trust procurement contracts, vendor partnership agreements, or financial budgets.
🚫 Legal & Security Sensitive: Legal advice regarding clinical negligence, disciplinary proceedings, passwords, or system access credentials.
Find more →




Types of Context
Explicit Context. Information you directly provide to the LLM, for example:

Your role and organization
The purpose of the task
Target audience

Implicit Context. Assumptions the LLM makes based on your prompt, for example:

Cultural assumptions
Educational level expectations

Language formality







Making Implicit Context Explicit



Instead of assuming the LLM will understand your context, state it clearly:
Instead of

Help me write an application for a fellowship

Try

I am a Specialty Registrar in cardiology applying for a MRC Clinical Research Training Fellowship. Help me draft a 3‑page Case for Support and a 1‑page Training & Development Plan tailored to this scheme.





Working Within Context Limits
LLMs have context windows, limits on how much text they can process at once or over different iterations. Some practical strategies to overcome this limitation are:

Summarize lengthy background information and prioritize the most important context
Break complex tasks into smaller parts
Use previous outputs as context for follow-up requests



Iterative Context Building
We will not always get what we want at the first attempt. A useful strategy is starting with basic context and refine:

Initial request: Provide core context
Review output: Identify what’s missing or wrong
Refine context: Add specific details or corrections
Iterate: Repeat until satisfactory





Exercise 2: Context Writing
Transform a vague prompt into an effective, contextualised request. Use an AI tool of your choice to observe the difference that context have on your request.
Scenario: You are a specialist registrar drafting a patient letter based on clinical notes.






Sample Clinical Notes





These notes are invented for medical education purposes and do not represent a real patient.
Patient: [SAMPLE PATIENT]
Age: 45F
Date: 03/01/2026


Presenting Complaint
6-month history of progressive fatigue, unintentional weight gain (4kg), and cold intolerance. Also experiencing hot flashes x 8 months which she initially attributed to perimenopause.


History of Presenting Complaint
Symptoms started gradually last summer with hot flashes occurring 4-5 times daily. Over subsequent months developed:

Persistent fatigue not relieved by rest
Weight gain despite no dietary changes
Cold intolerance, particularly hands and feet
Dry skin and thinning, brittle hair
Constipation (bowels now every 3-4 days, previously daily)
Brain fog - feels “slowed down” mentally, colleagues have noticed changes in productivity

No neck pain, dysphagia, voice changes, or recent viral illness.


Past Medical History

Hypercholesterolemia (diagnosed 2018) - managed with atorvastatin 20mg
Otherwise well



Medications

Atorvastatin 20mg OD
Paracetamol PRN for headaches

Allergies: NKDA


Family History

Sister diagnosed with Graves’ disease aged 38 (significant for autoimmune thyroid disease)
Mother: T2DM, hypertension
Father: IHD



Social History
Non-smoker, alcohol 6-8 units/week. Works as secondary school teacher. Lives with husband and two teenage children.



Examination
Vital Signs:

BP 128/82 | HR 58 bpm (regular) | Temp 36.4°C
Weight 74kg (previous 70kg six months ago) | BMI 27.3

Thyroid Examination:
Small, diffusely enlarged thyroid gland, non-tender with smooth texture. No discrete nodules palpable. No lymphadenopathy or bruit.
Other Findings:

Delayed relaxation phase of ankle reflexes (typical hypothyroid sign)
Dry skin noted on extremities
Bradycardia
CVS and respiratory exam otherwise unremarkable




Investigations (28/12/2025)
Thyroid Function Tests:

TSH: 12.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0) ↑↑
Free T4: 8.2 pmol/L (9-25) ↓
Free T3: 3.1 pmol/L (3.5-6.5) ↓

Thyroid Antibodies:

Anti-TPO: 486 IU/mL (<35) ↑↑↑ - strongly positive
Anti-thyroglobulin: 152 IU/mL (<40) ↑

Liver Function Tests:

ALT: 67 U/L (10-40) ↑
AST: 58 U/L (10-40) ↑
ALP, bilirubin, albumin, GGT - all within normal limits

Lipid Profile:

Total Cholesterol: 6.8 mmol/L (elevated despite statin therapy)
LDL: 4.2 mmol/L | HDL: 1.6 mmol/L | Triglycerides: 2.2 mmol/L

Full Blood Count:Normal (Hb 128 g/L, WCC 6.8, platelets 245)
Renal Function & Electrolytes: Normal (Cr 68, eGFR >90, Na 139, K 4.2)
Glucose Metabolism: Normal (fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L, HbA1c 36 mmol/mol)



Assessment
Primary hypothyroidism secondary to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
This patient presents with classical hypothyroid symptoms (fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, cognitive slowing, bradycardia) confirmed biochemically with elevated TSH and reduced thyroid hormones. The markedly elevated anti-TPO antibodies (>10x upper limit) strongly support Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Positive family history of autoimmune thyroid disease (sister with Graves’) and diffusely enlarged smooth thyroid gland are consistent with this diagnosis.
The mildly elevated transaminases are likely related to hypothyroidism itself - this commonly causes hepatic dysfunction that typically resolves with thyroid hormone replacement. Similarly, the elevated cholesterol despite statin therapy is a known consequence of untreated hypothyroidism.
Hot flashes are likely perimenopausal symptoms occurring concurrently, though will reassess once euthyroid as thyroid dysfunction can occasionally affect temperature regulation.



Management Plan
1. Thyroid Hormone Replacement
Starting levothyroxine 50 micrograms once daily. Using lower starting dose given cardiovascular risk factors (hypercholesterolemia). Advised to take on empty stomach 30 minutes before breakfast, avoiding calcium/iron supplements within 4 hours.
2. Monitoring Strategy

Recheck TFTs in 6-8 weeks (TSH and Free T4)
Aim for TSH in lower half of reference range (0.4-2.5 mIU/L)
Titrate dose in 25 microgram increments based on results
Recheck LFTs at 3 months to confirm improvement
Reassess lipid profile once euthyroid - may be able to adjust statin dose






Initial prompt

Write a letter to explain a medical condition and treatment







Solution example






Initial prompt

Write a letter to explain a medical condition and treatment

See Microsoft Copilot (GPT-5) answer here






See Microsoft Copilot (GPT-5) answer here





This letter is invented for medical education purposes and do not represent a real patient.
Date: 03/01/2026
Patient: [SAMPLE PATIENT], 45F
To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing to provide a summary of [Patient Name]’s recent medical assessment and treatment plan.
Medical Condition
The patient has been diagnosed with primary hypothyroidism secondary to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the thyroid gland, leading to reduced thyroid hormone production. This diagnosis is supported by clinical symptoms and laboratory findings:
Symptoms: Persistent fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, brittle hair, constipation, and cognitive slowing.
Examination: Bradycardia, delayed ankle reflexes, and a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland.
Investigations:

TSH: 12.4 mIU/L (elevated)
Free T4: 8.2 pmol/L (low)
Anti-TPO antibodies: 486 IU/mL (markedly elevated)

These findings confirm hypothyroidism and strongly indicate Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.
Treatment Plan
The patient has been started on levothyroxine 50 micrograms once daily, taken on an empty stomach 30 minutes before breakfast. This medication replaces the deficient thyroid hormone and will help restore normal metabolic function. Monitoring
Thyroid function tests will be repeated in 6–8 weeks to adjust the dose as needed.
Liver function and lipid profile will be reassessed after achieving a stable thyroid state.
Additional Notes
The patient’s mildly elevated liver enzymes and cholesterol are likely secondary to hypothyroidism and are expected to improve with treatment. Hot flashes may be related to perimenopause but will be reassessed once thyroid function normalizes.
If you require further details or clarification, please do not hesitate to contact me.
Sincerely,
[Your Name]
[Your Position]
[Contact Information]





Contextualised prompt
We want to use a tone that is empathetic and use simple language to explain the medical condition and prognosis.

Context. I am a Specialist Registrar in an NHS outpatient clinic drafting a letter to the patient after today’s appointment. I will provide the model with structured clinical notes.
Purpose. Create a clear, empathetic, patient‑friendly letter that explains the diagnosis and likely prognosis, outlines the agreed plan, and gives practical next steps.
Audience. The patient (and their family/carers), using plain English and UK spelling. Assume no clinical background. Tone & Style. Warm, respectful, and reassuring. Avoid jargon; define any necessary medical terms. Target a reading level suitable for the general public. Use short sentences and clear headings.
Safety & Governance. Do not invent facts; only use information present in the notes. Flag uncertainty transparently.
Privacy. Do not include sensitive details beyond what is needed to communicate care.
Format. One page. Include:

Sections: “What we discussed today”, “Your diagnosis explained”, “What this means for you”, “Your treatment and monitoring plan”, “Follow‑up and contacts”.
Bullet points for actions the patient should take.

Output. Return only the drafted letter content (no meta commentary).







See Microsoft Copilot (GPT-5) answer here





This letter is invented for medical education purposes and do not represent a real patient.
[Patient Name] Date: 03/01/2026
Dear [Patient Name],
Thank you for coming in today.
What we discussed today
You told me about feeling very tired for several months, gaining weight without changing your diet, feeling cold, and having dry skin and constipation. You also mentioned hot flushes, which started earlier.
Your blood tests and examination helped us understand what is causing these symptoms.
Your diagnosis explained
You have a condition called hypothyroidism, which means your thyroid gland is not making enough thyroid hormone. This hormone controls energy, temperature, and metabolism.
The tests show this is due to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, an autoimmune condition where your immune system attacks the thyroid gland. This is common and treatable.
What this means for you
With the right treatment, most people feel much better. The tiredness, weight changes, and other symptoms usually improve over weeks to months. This is a long-term condition, but it can be managed well with medication and regular monitoring.
Your treatment and monitoring plan
Start levothyroxine 50 micrograms once daily.
Take it on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before breakfast. Avoid taking calcium or iron supplements within 4 hours of your dose.
We will check your thyroid blood tests again in 6–8 weeks and adjust the dose if needed. We will also recheck your liver tests and cholesterol once your thyroid levels are stable.
Follow‑up and contacts
Blood test in 6–8 weeks (we will send you the details). Review appointment after your next blood test.
If you have questions or new symptoms, contact your GP or our clinic on [Clinic Phone Number].
Sincerely,
[Your Name]
[Your Position]
[Contact Information]

title: Privacy & Compliance
text:
Key Takeaways




Follow Hospital Group guidelines - Ensure compliance with mandatory frameworks, maintain transparency, document AI use appropriately
Never share sensitive data - No patient identifiable data, unpublished research, or confidential information in unapproved systems
Use the SAFE framework - Stick to approved tools, Always review outputs, Follow professional integrity, Enter minimal data
Assess risk and seek approval - Contact Information Governance for high-risk processing; DPIA mandatory for automated decision-making
Artificial Intelligence is increasingly embedded in healthcare tools and systems, and it isn’t always obvious when AI is operating in the background. Used appropriately, AI can improve clinical decision-making, streamline workflows, and enhance patient outcomes. However, AI also introduces significant compliance and safety risks, particularly when processing patient data or influencing clinical decisions.
As healthcare professionals working within North Bristol NHS Trust (NBT) and University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust (UHBW), you must understand what constitutes compliant AI use, when to seek guidance from Information Governance teams, and why awareness of “hidden AI” is critical to patient safety.

title: Privacy & Compliance
text:
Mandatory Compliance Framework
All AI systems used within the Hospital Group must comply with:

Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR
NHS Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC)
Clinical Safety Standards (DCB0129 and DCB0160)
Equality Act 2010
MHRA regulations (where applicable to medical devices)
NHS England AI guidance
Hospital Group AI Policy (HG-IG-001)

This applies to AI systems used for:

Direct patient care (e.g., clinical decision-making, diagnostics)
Operational purposes (e.g., workforce management, scheduling)
Administrative tasks (e.g., automated processes, documentation)
Research and innovation







Consequences of Non-Compliance



Failure to comply with this policy may result in:

Disciplinary action for staff
Termination of AI projects
Regulatory investigation for legislative breaches
Professional accountability implications

title: Privacy & Compliance
text:
The SAFE Framework for Healthcare
When using AI tools in clinical practice, remember to stay SAFE:

S – Stick to approved tools
Use only platforms approved by Trust procurement that meet clinical safety standards.

Approved tools operate within secure NHS infrastructure
Unapproved AI tools or “hidden AI” features pose high compliance and safety risks
Never use consumer-grade AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, public cloud services) with patient data
If uncertain, contact the Digital Services & Technology Team or Information Governance Team



A – Always review outputs
Clinicians remain responsible for all clinical decisions, regardless of AI involvement.

AI must never replace clinical judgment – you are accountable for patient care
A “human-in-the-loop” is required to mitigate clinical negligence risks
Review all outputs for accuracy, bias, and clinical appropriateness
AI can hallucinate information or perpetuate biases from training data
Treat AI outputs as clinical decision support, not diagnostic certainty



F – Follow Professional Integrity
Transparency is essential in clinical practice and research.

Disclose AI use in clinical records where relevant to patient care
Document AI-assisted decisions with clear rationale
In research contexts, declare AI use in methodology sections
Professional bodies (GMC, NMC, etc.) require transparent decision-making



E – Enter minimal data
Protect patient confidentiality at all times.

Strictly avoid entering Personal Identifiable Data (PID) into general-purpose LLMs
Never input sensitive health records, patient identifiers, or confidential information into unapproved systems
PID must never be forwarded to any address other than those ending in @nbt.nhs.uk or @uhbw.nhs.uk
Minimize personal data processing (data minimization principle)
Consider pseudonymisation or anonymisation where appropriate

Why SAFE matters: Using unapproved tools violates data protection law and Trust policy. You remain professionally and legally accountable for patient care. Breaching patient confidentiality violates UK GDPR, professional codes, and patient trust.

title: Privacy & Compliance
text:
Privacy Risk Assessment
Before using AI with any data, assess the privacy risk level:

Low Risk ✅

Public information already in the public domain
Generic clinical concepts without patient specifics
Educational materials with no identifiable information



Medium Risk ⚠️

Internal documents without personal data
Anonymized or aggregated data (properly anonymized)
Draft administrative content with no patient identifiers



High Risk ❌

Any personal or patient identifiable data
Confidential health records
Research data with identifiers
Unpublished clinical information
Financial or security credentials







Never Share in AI Systems




Patient names, NHS numbers, dates of birth, addresses
Medical record numbers or hospital identifiers
Clinical notes, test results, imaging with identifiers
Unpublished research data with personal information
Staff personal data or security credentials
Financial information or passwords

title: Privacy & Compliance
text:
When to Involve Information Governance
Not all AI use is low risk. You must contact the Information Governance Team or AI Governance Group before using AI if:

AI will process large volumes of patient data, especially special category data (health records, genetic data, mental health information)
AI will make or influence decisions about patients (e.g., diagnosis, treatment planning, triage, resource allocation)
You plan to combine multiple datasets for profiling or predictive analytics
The AI application is novel, complex, or feels high-risk
You are considering a new AI tool or using an approved tool in an untested way
You are developing a new AI model for research or clinical use

title: Privacy & Compliance
section: Best Practices for Safe AI Use
text:
Best Practices for Safe AI Use
Before using AI:

Verify the tool is approved for your intended use
Assess the privacy risk level of your data
Understand the AI system’s limitations and potential biases

During AI use:

Use institutional accounts (e.g., @nbt.nhs.uk) where available
Minimize data entered – only what’s necessary
Never include patient identifiers or sensitive data in unapproved systems
Review outputs critically before using them

After AI use:

Document AI use in clinical records where relevant
Report any concerns about AI performance or safety

title: Ethics & Environmental Impact
text:
Key Takeaways




Environmental sustainability is critical - Align AI use with NHS Net Zero commitments; use AI efficiently and choose appropriate models.
AI can perpetuate health inequalities - Watch for biases affecting patient outcomes; ensure equitable care for diverse populations.
Maintain clinical oversight - AI should enhance, not replace, clinical expertise and professional judgment.
Transparency builds trust - AI-influenced decisions must be explainable and auditable to patients and regulators.

title: Ethics & Environmental Impact
section: Environmental Impact and NHS Net Zero Commitments
text:
Environmental Impact and NHS Net Zero Commitments
The NHS has committed to “Delivering a Net Zero Health Service” with ambitious targets:

Net zero for controlled emissions by 2040 (direct NHS carbon footprint)
Net zero for influenced emissions by 2045 (wider supply chain and services)

As a healthcare professional, you must be mindful of environmental impacts when using AI tools. AI systems consume significant energy and natural resources, contributing to the NHS carbon footprint.

The Full Environmental Cost of AI
AI’s environmental impact extends beyond initial model training to encompass the entire life cycle: raw material extraction, manufacturing, training, deployment (inference), and disposal.
Training Phase: Large language models require intensive computational resources. For example, GPT-3’s training produced an estimated 85,000 kg of CO₂, equivalent to 112 cars running for a year.
Inference Phase: The ongoing deployment phase (when users interact with models) can exceed training emissions within weeks (Luccioni et al. 2024). Every clinical query, every patient interaction with AI, requires computational resources and energy.
Data Center Infrastructure: Generative AI is driving substantial growth in data centers, which have significant environmental costs:

Approximately 40% of data center energy goes toward cooling processing units
AI systems consume vast amounts of fresh water for cooling
ChatGPT consumes approximately half a liter of fresh water for every chat of 20–50 prompts (Li et al. 2025)







Water Scarcity and Healthcare Sustainability



Two-thirds of new data centers built in the USA since 2022 are located in areas already experiencing water scarcity. As healthcare professionals committed to health equity, we must consider how AI infrastructure impacts vulnerable communities globally.




Sustainable AI Practices in Clinical Settings
Given the NHS Net Zero commitments and the significant consumption required for AI deployment, focusing on efficiency is essential:
Reduce Usage:

Use AI for high-value clinical tasks where it demonstrably improves patient outcomes or safety
Avoid using AI for trivial tasks that can be completed efficiently without computational resources
Batch similar queries together when appropriate
Cache and reuse outputs when possible (ensuring compliance with data governance)

Choose Efficiently:

Consider the computational cost of AI requests in clinical workflows
Use smaller, more efficient models when they meet clinical needs
Support Trust procurement decisions that prioritize providers committed to renewable energy
Consider whether AI use aligns with NHS sustainability goals







Clinical Context Matters



Ask yourself: Does this AI use deliver meaningful patient benefit that justifies its environmental cost? If a traditional method achieves the same outcome with lower resource consumption, that may be the more sustainable choice.
It is acceptable to choose not to use AI based on ethical and environmental factors

title: Ethics & Environmental Impact
text:
Bias, Equity, and Patient Outcomes
AI systems can inherit and amplify existing health inequalities. The Hospital Group AI Policy mandates that all AI systems be evaluated for bias to prevent discrimination and ensure equitable care for diverse patient populations.
Health inequalities are well-documented across multiple dimensions, and AI systems trained on biased data can perpetuate or worsen these disparities. As clinicians, we have a professional and ethical duty to ensure AI does not compromise equitable patient care.






Bias Detection Questions for Clinical AI



When reviewing AI outputs or implementing AI systems, ask:

Representation: Which patient groups are included or excluded in the training data?
Outcomes: Does this AI perform equally well across different demographic groups?
Language: Are clinical descriptions fair and respectful to all patients?
Assumptions: What unstated assumptions is the AI making about patients?
Access: Can all patients benefit from this AI equally, or does it create new barriers?
Validation: Has this AI been validated in populations similar to our diverse patient cohort?

title: Ethics & Environmental Impact
text:
Transparency and Explainability
The Hospital Group AI Policy mandates that AI decision-making processes must be auditable, transparent, and explainable. This is fundamental to maintaining patient trust and meeting professional accountability standards.

Why Transparency Matters
Patient Autonomy: Patients have the right to understand how clinical decisions affecting their care are made, including when AI is involved.
Clinical Accountability: As the responsible clinician, you must be able to explain your reasoning to patients, colleagues, and regulators—including how AI influenced your decisions.
Public Trust: The NHS depends on public confidence. Opaque AI systems that cannot be explained undermine trust in healthcare.


Explainability in Practice
When AI influences clinical decisions:

Record in patient notes when AI tools have been used
Explain how AI information contributed to your clinical reasoning
Inform patients when AI has contributed to their care pathway







“Black Box” AI Is Not Acceptable



If you cannot explain how an AI system reached a recommendation in plain language to a patient or colleague, it may not meet Trust requirements for transparency. Escalate concerns about unexplainable AI to the AI Governance Group.

title: Ethics & Environmental Impact
text:
Other Ethical Considerations
Beyond bias and environmental concerns, AI use in healthcare raises important ethical questions about data rights, labor practices, and the value of human clinical judgment.

Data Rights and Consent
Large language models are typically trained on vast datasets collected without explicit consent from content creators or data subjects. This raises particular concerns in healthcare:

Patient Data: Ensure no patient data enters unapproved AI systems without appropriate consent and governance
Research Data: Respect data sharing agreements and patient consent for secondary use
Intellectual Property: Academic medical literature used in AI training may lack proper attribution



Labor Practices in AI Development
AI development relies heavily on labor that is often invisible to clinical users:

Content Moderation: Workers, often in lower-income countries, review harmful content and rate AI outputs
Data Annotation: Medical AI systems require expert annotation, which may be inadequately compensated
Global Inequity: AI benefits accrue to high-income healthcare settings while burdens (environmental, labor) affect vulnerable populations globally

As NHS professionals committed to social justice, we should be aware of these structural inequities.


The Value of Clinical Judgment and Human Connection
The appropriateness of AI use extends beyond technical performance to consider the intrinsic value of human clinical judgment and the therapeutic relationship.
Clinical Judgment Cannot Be Automated:

Pattern recognition algorithms cannot replicate the holistic assessment of experienced clinicians
Clinical intuition, developed through years of practice, integrates subtle cues AI may miss
Professional judgment includes ethical reasoning and values that AI cannot capture

The Therapeutic Relationship Matters:

Patient trust depends on genuine human connection and empathy
Using AI to generate clinical correspondence may signal you do not value the patient interaction equally
Compassionate communication requires authentic human engagement, not algorithmic efficiency

Professional Development:

Clinical expertise develops through deliberate practice and reflective thinking
Over-reliance on AI may atrophy clinical skills, particularly in junior doctors
The process of clinical reasoning is as valuable as the diagnostic conclusion

Reliability and Safety:

AI outputs may contain errors, hallucinations, or unverifiable claims
The effort required to verify AI recommendations may exceed independent clinical decision-making
Patient safety depends on your ability to critically evaluate AI outputs, not accept them uncritically







Maintain Human Primacy in Clinical Care



AI should enhance your clinical capabilities, not replace your judgment. If you find yourself deferring to AI rather than thinking critically, step back and reassert your clinical autonomy. Your patients deserve your full professional engagement.

title: What are LLMs?
text:
Key Takeaways




LLMs are mathematical models of language that maps similar words to nearby positions in a conceptual space

They predict which words are most likely to follow a given input, or prompt, based on patterns learned from vast amounts of text
They work by pattern matching, not true understanding, therefore they are not infallible sources of truth

Always verify important information from authoritative sources
Be aware of bias in AI outputs and actively check for it
Use critical thinking - if something sounds too precise or extreme, investigate further
Always follow your workplace guidance




Natural Language Processing
Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a branch of Artificial Intelligence that serves as the foundational technology that enables Large Language Models to understand and generate human language. Natural language is inherently ambiguous and contextual.
Consider the sentence

“I saw the man with the telescope”.

This could mean:

you used a telescope to see the man,
or you saw a man carrying a telescope.

At its core, NLP transforms words, phrases, and sentences into numerical representations called embeddings—high-dimensional vectors that capture semantic meaning and relationships between linguistic elements. These embedding spaces are constructed so that words or phrases with similar meanings are positioned closer together in the vector space, while semantically different concepts are farther apart. For example, “king” and “man” would be nearby vectors, as would “queen” and “woman” but “man” and “woman” would be distant. This mathematical representation of language allows to perform some complex reasoning about text by manipulating these vectors through neural network operations.



A simple 2D embedding space of the words: blue, king, man, pink, princess, queen, woman.




The Large Language Model Revolution
Large Language Models represented a paradigm shift in learning language patterns from the Internet, books, and other vast text sources. Built on transformer architecture, LLMs focus on relevant parts of the input when processing words (tokens) or phrases, enabling understanding of long-range dependencies that earlier models missed. While you don’t need to understand the mathematics, the key insight is that LLMs work by finding patterns and relationships between concepts.
Let’s assume that we want to embed the words of this sentence:

The Jean Golding Institute is a central hub for data science and data-intensive research at the University of Bristol. We connect a multidisciplinary community of experts across the University and beyond.

Our chatbot will break the sentence in tokens of one or less words and assign each a numeric identifier, as depicted below. A rule of thumb is that one token generally corresponds to 4 characters of text for common English.




Text is broken into words or token. “A helpful rule of thumb is that one token generally corresponds to ~4 characters of text for common English text”. Source: https://platform.openai.com/tokenizer


Each of these tokens will have a mapping in the embedding space of our LLM model.



Multidimensional embedding space example.


What makes LLMs “large” is their training scale, the exposure to hundreds of billions of words from diverse sources allows them to internalize grammar, vocabulary, world knowledge, and reasoning patterns. The training process is elegantly simple: models learn by predicting the next word in sequences, adjusting internal parameters based on prediction errors. This forces development of sophisticated internal representations of language and knowledge.
LLMs fundamentally change how we approach NLP tasks. Instead of building specialized systems for each application, a single LLM can handle multiple tasks through different prompting strategies. The same model that excels at translation can also summarize documents, answer questions, or generate creative content without additional training.
The workplace implications are profound. Tasks requiring specialized software and technical expertise become accessible through natural language interaction. Document analysis, content generation, customer service automation, and data extraction are now available to non-technical users through conversational interfaces.


What can LLMs do?
LLMs can help with:

Writing assistance: Drafting emails, reports, and documents
Summarization: Condensing long texts into key points

Translation: Converting between languages
Question answering: Providing information on various topics
Code generation: Writing and explaining programming code
Creative tasks: Brainstorming ideas and creative writing







LLM Limitations



However, LLMs introduce new challenges. LLMs “reproduce bias and stereotyping, hallucinates, and makes mistakes” and require “discernment and the critical faculties of a human being to evaluate outputs.”
LLM Limitations

Hallucinations. LLMs can generate plausible-sounding but entirely incorrect information.
Bias. LLMs reflect biases present in their training data.
Mistakes. LLMs can make subtle errors that are difficult to detect without domain expertise.

Why These Limitations Matter?

Professional Responsibility. Errors in your work can have serious consequences.
Academic Integrity. Using unverified AI-generated content violates scholarly standards.
Ethical Obligations. Propagating bias can harm individuals and communities.
Legal Implications. Incorrect information in professional contexts can create liability.

Find more →








Good Practice Examples



AI should enhance your capabilities, not replace your thinking:
✅ Research Assistant: “Help me identify key themes in these interview transcripts I’ve analyzed”
✅ Writing Coach: “Suggest ways to improve clarity in this paragraph I wrote”
✅ Brainstorm Partner: “What questions should I consider when designing this survey?”
✅ Editor: “Check this draft for logical flow and suggest improvements”






Exercise 1: Identifying LLM Limitations
Scenario: You’re preparing a briefing document about climate change impacts in Bristol.
Prompt:

Write 2 sentences about how climate change is impacting Bristol

Review the below outputs of three different LLM tools and identify potential issues:

Which output seems most reliable and why?
What red flags can you identify in each response?
How would you verify the information before using it professionally?


Output A: “Bristol experienced its wettest year on record in 2023, with rainfall 40% above average. The Severn Estuary’s sea level has risen 15cm since 2000, directly threatening the city center.”

Output B: “Climate change will cause Bristol’s temperature to increase by exactly 3.2°C by 2050, making it uninhabitable for most residents. The city council has already approved plans to relocate the entire population to higher ground.”

Output C: “Bristol faces increased flooding risks due to climate change. The city has implemented various adaptation measures, though specific impacts vary by neighborhood and depend on global emission scenarios.”






Solution example





Output A: “Bristol experienced its wettest year on record in 2023, with rainfall 40% above average. The Severn Estuary’s sea level has risen 15cm since 2000, directly threatening the city center.”
Contains specific statistics that need verification. While plausible, the exact figures should be fact-checked against official sources.
⚠️ Specific statistics require verification: “Wettest year on record” and “40% above average” are precise claims that need fact-checking
⚠️ Sea level measurement: The specific “15cm since 2000” figure should be verified against official sources
⚠️ Causal claim: Direct threat to city center needs geographic verification
✅ Generally plausible: The types of impacts described are consistent with climate science

Output B: “Climate change will cause Bristol’s temperature to increase by exactly 3.2°C by 2050, making it uninhabitable for most residents. The city council has already approved plans to relocate the entire population to higher ground.”
Contains obvious hallucinations - overly precise predictions and extreme claims about population relocation that aren’t realistic.
🚫 Unrealistic precision: “Exactly 3.2°C” - climate models deal in ranges, not exact predictions
🚫 Extreme claims: “Uninhabitable for most residents” is hyperbolic and unsupported
🚫 False information: No evidence of city council relocation plans
🚫 Hallucination: Appears to invent specific policy decisions

Output C: “Bristol faces increased flooding risks due to climate change. The city has implemented various adaptation measures, though specific impacts vary by neighborhood and depend on global emission scenarios.”
Most reliable approach - acknowledges uncertainty, speaks in general terms about known issues, doesn’t make unsupported specific claims.
✅ Appropriately general: Makes broad, supportable statements
✅ Acknowledges uncertainty: “Vary by neighborhood” and “depend on scenarios”
✅ Realistic scope: Doesn’t make unsupported specific claims
✅ Professional tone: Appropriate for briefing document

Key Learning Points:

Be suspicious of overly precise statistics without sources
Extreme or alarmist language often indicates hallucination
The most useful AI outputs acknowledge uncertainty appropriately
Always verify specific factual claims before using professionally

title: Introduction
text:
Welcome to this training course on the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in healthcare.
The term Artificial Intelligence refers to computer systems that can perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognising patterns, and making decisions. While the AI field has many years of research and development behind it, today’s increased popularity is largely driven by generative AI models—systems that can create new content like text, images, and code based on the patterns they’ve learned from vast amounts of data. You’ve probably heard of and used tools like ChatGPT and Copilot—here we’ll learn how to use them effectively, safely, and in compliance with workplace policies and NHS guidance.






Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy at NBT & UHBW (HG-IG-001)



This course is built on the foundation of the Hospital Group’s commitment to responsible AI adoption that transforms healthcare delivery while maintaining the highest standards of safety, ethics, and compliance.
Core Principles for AI Use:

Patient Safety First: All AI systems must be tested, validated, and continuously monitored for safety and effectiveness
Transparency & Explainability: AI decision-making processes must be auditable, transparent, and explainable to patients and clinicians
Ethical Use & Bias Mitigation: All AI systems must be evaluated for bias to ensure equitable care for diverse patient populations
Human Oversight: AI systems must have defined human accountability for decisions, particularly those affecting patient care
Compliance: All AI systems must comply with UK GDPR, Data Protection Act 2018, NHS Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC), and clinical safety standards

Find more information →



Learning Objectives
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

Understand what LLMs are and their key capabilities and limitations
Apply responsible practices when using AI tools in your work
Craft effective prompts that enhance rather than replace critical thinking
Navigate ethical considerations including bias, privacy, and environmental impact



About this course
These course materials have been designed and developed by Pau Erola, PhD (Jean Golding Institute, University of Bristol).
Thanks to Huw Day for his feedback and recommendations on ethics and environmental impact. Thanks to Leo Gorman, Will Chapman, Rita Rasteiro, Richard Lane, James Thomas and Patricia Holley for their valuable comments and corrections.
We used the enhancement of AI in alignment with our institutional guidance:

Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4 & GPT-5)– Generation of synthetic datasets, documents and examples
Claude (Sonnet 4) – Writing assistance, examples generation
ChatGPT (GPT-5) – Generation of figures

For queries related to this course please contact jgi-training@bristol.ac.uk.

title: Harnessing AI in healthcare
text:
These notes are invented for medical education purposes and do not represent a real patient.
Patient: [SAMPLE PATIENT]
Age: 45F
Date: 03/01/2026


Presenting Complaint
6-month history of progressive fatigue, unintentional weight gain (4kg), and cold intolerance. Also experiencing hot flashes x 8 months which she initially attributed to perimenopause.


History of Presenting Complaint
Symptoms started gradually last summer with hot flashes occurring 4-5 times daily. Over subsequent months developed:

Persistent fatigue not relieved by rest
Weight gain despite no dietary changes
Cold intolerance, particularly hands and feet
Dry skin and thinning, brittle hair
Constipation (bowels now every 3-4 days, previously daily)
Brain fog - feels “slowed down” mentally, colleagues have noticed changes in productivity

No neck pain, dysphagia, voice changes, or recent viral illness.


Past Medical History

Hypercholesterolemia (diagnosed 2018) - managed with atorvastatin 20mg
Otherwise well



Medications

Atorvastatin 20mg OD
Paracetamol PRN for headaches

Allergies: NKDA


Family History

Sister diagnosed with Graves’ disease aged 38 (significant for autoimmune thyroid disease)
Mother: T2DM, hypertension
Father: IHD



Social History
Non-smoker, alcohol 6-8 units/week. Works as secondary school teacher. Lives with husband and two teenage children.



Examination
Vital Signs:

BP 128/82 | HR 58 bpm (regular) | Temp 36.4°C
Weight 74kg (previous 70kg six months ago) | BMI 27.3

Thyroid Examination:
Small, diffusely enlarged thyroid gland, non-tender with smooth texture. No discrete nodules palpable. No lymphadenopathy or bruit.
Other Findings:

Delayed relaxation phase of ankle reflexes (typical hypothyroid sign)
Dry skin noted on extremities
Bradycardia
CVS and respiratory exam otherwise unremarkable




Investigations (28/12/2025)
Thyroid Function Tests:

TSH: 12.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0) ↑↑
Free T4: 8.2 pmol/L (9-25) ↓
Free T3: 3.1 pmol/L (3.5-6.5) ↓

Thyroid Antibodies:

Anti-TPO: 486 IU/mL (<35) ↑↑↑ - strongly positive
Anti-thyroglobulin: 152 IU/mL (<40) ↑

Liver Function Tests:

ALT: 67 U/L (10-40) ↑
AST: 58 U/L (10-40) ↑
ALP, bilirubin, albumin, GGT - all within normal limits

Lipid Profile:

Total Cholesterol: 6.8 mmol/L (elevated despite statin therapy)
LDL: 4.2 mmol/L | HDL: 1.6 mmol/L | Triglycerides: 2.2 mmol/L

Full Blood Count:Normal (Hb 128 g/L, WCC 6.8, platelets 245)
Renal Function & Electrolytes: Normal (Cr 68, eGFR >90, Na 139, K 4.2)
Glucose Metabolism: Normal (fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L, HbA1c 36 mmol/mol)



Assessment
Primary hypothyroidism secondary to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
This patient presents with classical hypothyroid symptoms (fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, cognitive slowing, bradycardia) confirmed biochemically with elevated TSH and reduced thyroid hormones. The markedly elevated anti-TPO antibodies (>10x upper limit) strongly support Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Positive family history of autoimmune thyroid disease (sister with Graves’) and diffusely enlarged smooth thyroid gland are consistent with this diagnosis.
The mildly elevated transaminases are likely related to hypothyroidism itself - this commonly causes hepatic dysfunction that typically resolves with thyroid hormone replacement. Similarly, the elevated cholesterol despite statin therapy is a known consequence of untreated hypothyroidism.
Hot flashes are likely perimenopausal symptoms occurring concurrently, though will reassess once euthyroid as thyroid dysfunction can occasionally affect temperature regulation.



Management Plan
1. Thyroid Hormone Replacement
Starting levothyroxine 50 micrograms once daily. Using lower starting dose given cardiovascular risk factors (hypercholesterolemia). Advised to take on empty stomach 30 minutes before breakfast, avoiding calcium/iron supplements within 4 hours.
2. Monitoring Strategy

Recheck TFTs in 6-8 weeks (TSH and Free T4)
Aim for TSH in lower half of reference range (0.4-2.5 mIU/L)
Titrate dose in 25 microgram increments based on results
Recheck LFTs at 3 months to confirm improvement
Reassess lipid profile once euthyroid - may be able to adjust statin dose

title: Prompting Frameworks
text:
Key Takeaways




High-quality prompts eliminate ambiguity - Clear context upfront gets better responses
Use structured frameworks, e.g. the CLEAR framework, to ensure complete prompts
Never share sensitive data - No personal records, confidential research, or security information



High-quality prompts that eliminate ambiguity are crucial for getting useful responses from Large Language Models. By providing comprehensive context upfront, you’re more likely to receive output that matches your requirements.
Scenario: You have been tasked with running a campaign to increase recruitment of European students for your University’s MSc Engineering programs.
You write the initial prompt:

Write something about recruiting staff

Problems with this prompt:

No context about the role, program, or target audience
Vague action (“write something”)
No specifics about format, length, or communication channel
No examples of desired output
Unclear what type of recruitment content is needed

We can use some frameworks to standardize our queries and make sure they are complete and don’t forget any relevant details. There’s no right or wrong approach — different frameworks may work better for different AI tools and yourself, so use the one that works better for you.

The CLEAR Framework
The CLEAR framework offers a systematic approach to prompt construction that ensures comprehensive communication with AI models.
Context - Establish the situation and background

Explain who you are and what you’re working on
Provide relevant background information about your project or industry
Include any important constraints or considerations

Length - Define output requirements

Specify how much content you want (word count, number of items, etc.)
Indicate format preferences (paragraphs, bullet points, sections)
Include any structural requirements

Examples - Illustrate desired outcomes

Show examples of the style or format you’re looking for
Provide sample inputs or scenarios when relevant
Include both positive examples (what you want) and negative examples (what to avoid)

Action - State the specific task

Clearly articulate what you want the AI to do
Use specific action verbs (create, analyze, summarize, compare)
Be direct and avoid ambiguous language
Focus on one primary task per prompt

Role - Define the AI’s perspective

Specify what expertise or viewpoint the AI should adopt
Indicate the audience the AI should write for
Guide the AI’s approach and decision-making framework

A good prompt example using the CLEAR framework:

Context: I work in the postgraduate admissions team at a UK university promoting Clinical Doctoral programmes for healthcare professionals (e.g., nurses, allied health professionals, pharmacists). These programmes combine advanced research training with clinical practice, aiming to improve patient care and health systems.
Length: Create a 250-350 word recruitment email with a compelling subject line and clear call-to-action.

Include a short testimonial format:
Dr Sarah, Clinical Doctoral Graduate: “This programme transformed my practice and opened doors to leadership roles.”

Avoid: heavy academic jargon or generic phrases like “apply now for exciting opportunities.”

Action: Write a recruitment email encouraging healthcare professionals to apply for our Clinical Doctoral PhD programmes. Highlight benefits such as impact on patient care, career progression, flexible study options, and strong NHS links. Address common concerns about time commitment and funding.
Role: Act as an experienced postgraduate recruitment specialist who understands healthcare professionals’ priorities: improving patient outcomes, advancing their career, and managing work-life balance. Inspire confidence that this is a worthwhile investment in their future and their profession.







AI Policy at NBT & UHBW (HG-IG-001)



Independently of the prompting framework you are using, never share these with unapproved or general-purpose AI tools:
🚫 Personal Identifiable Data (PID): Patient medical records, health status, NHS numbers, or staff personal files.
🚫 Sensitive Clinical Information: Diagnostic scans, consultation transcripts (from AI Scribes), or unverified discharge summaries.
🚫 Confidential Medical Research: Unpublished clinical trial findings, grant applications under review, or proprietary drug discovery data.
🚫 Commercially Sensitive Data: Trust procurement contracts, vendor partnership agreements, or financial budgets.
🚫 Legal & Security Sensitive: Legal advice regarding clinical negligence, disciplinary proceedings, passwords, or system access credentials.
Find more →






Exercise 3: Building CPD Agenda Prompt
Scenario: You’re organizing a Continuing Professional Development (CPD) session on “Managing Acute Coronary Syndrome in the Emergency Department” at North Bristol NHS Trust.
Task: Create a prompt to help design the CPD session agenda.
Requirements:

Use the CLEAR framework
Include appropriate constraints
Maintain clinical accuracy and patient safety focus
Ensure compliance with Trust governance

Reflection Questions:

How do your prompts ensure AI enhances rather than replaces your clinical expertise?
What verification steps would you take for each output (e.g., checking against current NICE guidelines)?
How would you document AI assistance in the CPD materials?







Solution example





Create a prompt to help design a CPD session on “Managing Acute Coronary Syndrome in the Emergency Department” at North Bristol NHS Trust.

Context: I’m an Emergency Medicine consultant organizing a CPD session on “Managing Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) in the Emergency Department” for junior doctors (FY2-ST3 level) and emergency nurse practitioners with varied experience in cardiology.
Length: Create a detailed 4-hour CPD agenda with 15-20 minute segments.
Examples: Include interactive elements like case-based discussions, ECG interpretation stations, and small group simulation scenarios, similar to effective clinical teaching sessions using flipped classroom approaches.
Action: Design an agenda that balances didactic teaching, case discussions, and practical skills practice, progressing from initial assessment to definitive management and decision-making.
Role: Act as an experienced clinical educator specializing in emergency medicine and acute care teaching.
Additional Constraints:

Maximum 15 participants to allow for meaningful case discussion and skill practice.

Must align with current NICE guidelines on ACS management (CG94, NG185).

Reference must be made to MONA (Morphine, Oxygen, Nitrates, Aspirin) protocol and current evidence base.
Include time for discussion of local Trust protocols and pathways.

Consider multidisciplinary learning needs (doctors and nurses).

Include clinical governance elements: learning outcomes, evaluation methods, and CPD certification requirements.

Build in time for questions and clarification of complex cases.

title: Conversational Learning
text:
Key Takeaways




Use AI as learning partner, not task executor - Ask “why” and “how” to understand processes, not just get outputs
Shift from efficiency to learning mindset - Move from “give me the answer” to “walk me through the thinking”
Challenge AI reasoning - Test explanations, ask about limitations, play devil’s advocate



Most people approach AI with a transactional mindset, asking for document summaries, presentation outlines, email drafts, or quick recommendations. While this approach produces immediate outputs, it creates a fundamental problem: you receive results without gaining insight into the underlying processes that created them.
The learning partnership approach transforms this dynamic entirely. Instead of simply requesting outputs, you engage AI as a collaborative thinking partner. You might ask an AI to explain why it structured a summary in a particular way, what principles guided its outline choices, or how it determined the appropriate tone for professional communication. This shift in questioning style ensures that every interaction becomes an opportunity to understand processes and develop transferable skills.






NHS 10-Year Health Plan



“NHS Trusts should ensure that AI does not replace clinical judgement to mitigate the risk of clinical negligence – there should always be a”human in the loop” to check and verify AI-generated outputs.”
Find more →


The difference in outcomes is profound. Traditional approaches leave you dependent on AI for similar future tasks, while learning partnerships build your capacity to handle increasingly complex challenges independently.

The Power of “Why” Questions
Understanding decision-making processes is at the heart of conversational learning. Rather than accepting AI outputs at face value, successful learners probe deeper into the reasoning behind recommendations. This approach reveals the thinking patterns and analytical frameworks that experts use in their fields.
Instead of just accepting AI outputs, explore the reasoning:








From
→
To




Efficiency Mindset
→
Learning Mindset


“Just tell me what to do”
→
“Help me understand why this works”


“Give me the answer”
→
“Walk me through the thinking process”


“What’s the best practice?”
→
“What are the trade-offs I should consider?”


Certainty Seeking
→
Uncertainty Embracing


“What’s the right answer?”
→
“What factors should influence this decision?”


“Tell me the best approach”
→
“Help me understand the complexity of this issue”









Remember



The goal isn’t to have AI solve your problems, but to help you become better at solving problems yourself. Every conversation should leave you more capable and knowledgeable than when you started.




Learning Questions
Process Questions. How did you do that?

“Walk me through your thinking process”
“What steps did you follow to reach this conclusion?”
“How did you prioritize these factors?”

Justification Questions. Why this approach?

“What makes this approach better than alternatives?”
“What assumptions underlie your recommendation?”
“Why did you emphasize this particular aspect?”

Alternative Questions. What else could work?

“What other approaches did you consider?”
“How would this change in different contexts?”
“What would you do if [constraint] existed?”

Critical Questions. What are the limitations?

“What are the potential weaknesses of this approach?”
“Where might this reasoning fall short?”
“What would a critic say about this recommendation?”

Challenging AI Reasoning. Don’t just accept explanations, test them.

“What would happen if we did the opposite?”
“Can you think of situations where this approach would fail?”
“What evidence would contradict your recommendation?”
“What’s the worst-case scenario with this approach?”
“Play devil’s advocate with your own suggestion”
“What would a skeptic say about this approach?”





Exercise 4: Conversational Learning Practice
Scenario: You need to improve staff participation in development courses.
1. Traditional Approach. First, ask AI directly: “Give me strategies to increase staff participation in development courses.”
2. Learning Partnership Approach. Now, have a learning conversation. Use these conversation starters:

Explore the problem: “Help me understand why staff might be reluctant to participate. What factors typically influence participation?”
Question assumptions: “I’m assuming low participation is a problem - help me examine this assumption. When might quiet classrooms actually be effective?”
Build understanding: “What principles of group dynamics and learning psychology should guide my approach?”

3. Reflection. Compare the two approaches:

Which gave you more insight into the underlying issues?
Which better prepared you to handle similar challenges in the future?







Solution example





Based on Copilot (GPT-4 architecture).

In 200 words, give me strategies to increase staff participation in development courses.







To increase staff participation in development courses, focus on relevance, accessibility, and motivation. Begin by aligning courses with individual career goals and team objectives. When staff see how training supports their growth or contributes to project success, they’re more likely to engage.
Make learning convenient by offering flexible formats—online modules, short sessions, or on-demand access. Ensure courses are scheduled during work hours and don’t conflict with key responsibilities.
Leadership plays a key role: managers should actively promote courses, participate themselves, and recognize staff who engage. This sets a positive example and reinforces a culture of learning.
Incentivize participation with certificates, digital badges, or public recognition. Link course completion to tangible benefits like eligibility for new roles or responsibilities.
Regularly communicate the value of development opportunities through internal channels. Use success stories or testimonials to show real-world impact.
Finally, gather feedback to improve course offerings and involve staff in shaping future content. When employees feel heard and see their input reflected, they’re more likely to participate.




In 200 words, help me understand why staff might be reluctant to participate. What factors typically influence participation?







Staff may be reluctant to participate in development courses due to a mix of practical constraints and psychological factors. One of the most common barriers is lack of time—employees often feel overwhelmed by daily responsibilities and may not see how training fits into their workload. If courses are scheduled during busy periods or require significant time commitments, participation drops.
Another key factor is perceived relevance. Staff are less likely to engage if they don’t see how the course content applies to their role or career goals. Generic or outdated offerings can feel disconnected from real work challenges.
Managerial support also plays a crucial role. If leaders don’t actively encourage participation or fail to prioritize learning, staff may assume it’s not valued. Conversely, when managers model engagement and link training to performance reviews or promotions, uptake improves.
Fear of failure or judgment can also deter participation, especially in group settings or courses with assessments. Some staff may worry about exposing gaps in their knowledge.
Finally, accessibility issues—such as limited formats, lack of remote options, or unclear instructions—can make courses hard to attend.




I’m assuming low participation is a problem - help me examine this assumption. When might quiet classrooms actually be effective? Don’t use more than 200 words.







Low participation in development courses is often seen as a problem, but it’s worth examining whether that assumption always holds. A quiet classroom doesn’t necessarily mean disengagement—it can reflect deep concentration, a preference for self-paced learning, or a mismatch between delivery style and learning preferences.
Some staff may prefer asynchronous formats, such as recorded sessions or written materials, which don’t require visible participation. Others may be absorbing content passively before applying it practically. In highly skilled or research-focused environments, staff might already be learning informally through projects, peer collaboration, or independent study.
Additionally, low attendance might indicate that the course isn’t needed, rather than a lack of interest. If staff already possess the skills being taught, or if the course doesn’t align with current priorities, opting out can be a rational choice.
Rather than focusing solely on numbers, it’s more useful to assess impact—are those who attend applying what they learn? Are staff developing in other ways? Quiet classrooms can still be effective if they support meaningful, relevant learning.




What principles of group dynamics and learning psychology should guide my approach? Don’t use more than 200 words.







Your approach to increasing participation in development courses should be guided by key principles from group dynamics and learning psychology:

Social Influence & Norms. People are more likely to engage when they see peers doing the same. Creating visible norms around participation—such as team-wide involvement or manager endorsement—can foster a sense of collective commitment.
Psychological Safety. Staff need to feel safe to ask questions, make mistakes, and share ideas. A supportive learning environment encourages participation, especially in group settings.
Self-Determination Theory. Motivation increases when learners feel autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Offer choices in course formats, ensure content builds confidence, and foster connection through collaborative activities.
Constructivist Learning. People learn best when they actively construct knowledge through experience. Encourage reflection, discussion, and application to real tasks rather than passive consumption.
Group Cohesion. Strong group bonds improve engagement. Use team-based learning, peer mentoring, or shared goals to build trust and accountability.

title: LLMs tools
text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have been rapidly introduced to workplace environments since ChatGPT’s breakthrough launch in late 2022. The landscape is quickly evolving, with major tech companies and AI startups releasing increasingly sophisticated models tailored for different use needs. When selecting an LLM consider factors such as data privacy policies, integration capabilities, cost structure, and specific feature sets that align with the University’s workflows. The following list covers the some of the most prominent options available today.






AI Policy at NBT & UHBW (HG-IG-001)



Use approved tools only — no AI may be used without prior approval.

Mandatory approval process: Follow the AI Implementation Process Map and engage the AI Governance Group, Caldicott Guardian, and Information Governance (IG) Team before any deployment.
Compliance standards: Tools must meet NHS DTAC, comply with UK GDPR, and (where applicable) MHRA medical device requirements.
Clinical safety first: AI must never replace clinical judgment. A human-in-the-loop must review and verify AI outputs.
Data residency & security: Ensure UK data sovereignty and alignment with the Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT).
Prohibited: Do not use unapproved tools or “hidden AI” features in software, due to compliance and privacy risks.

If in doubt: Stop and contact IG/AI Governance before using any AI functionality.
Find more →



Microsoft Copilot copilot.microsoft.com

First Release: March 2023
Strengths: Deep integration with Microsoft Office suite
Best for: Document creation, email assistance, Office workflows, enterprise productivity
Considerations: Enterprise versions offer better data protection; requires Microsoft 365 subscription



ChatGPT (OpenAI) chat.openai.com

First Release: November 2022
Strengths: Conversational, good for general tasks, coding assistance
Best for: Writing assistance, brainstorming, general Q&A, code generation
Considerations: Data usage policies vary by version; enterprise versions available



Claude (Anthropic) claude.ai

First Release: March 2023
Strengths: Helpful, harmless, honest approach; excellent for analysis
Best for: Analysis, research assistance, ethical reasoning, document processing
Considerations: Strong focus on safety and accuracy; large context window



Google Gemini gemini.google.com

First Release: December 2023
Strengths: Multimodal capabilities, integration with Google Workspace
Best for: Research, document analysis, creative tasks, Google ecosystem integration
Considerations: Various models available (Nano, Pro, Ultra) with different capabilities



Google NotebookLM notebooklm.google.com

First Release: July 2023
Strengths: Document-grounded AI, source-based research, podcast-style audio summaries
Best for: Research analysis, document synthesis, creating audio overviews, academic work
Considerations: Works with your uploaded sources; Plus version offers 5x higher usage limits



Perplexity AI perplexity.ai

First Release: August 2022
Strengths: Real-time web search integration, source citations
Best for: Research, fact-checking, current information retrieval
Considerations: Excellent for staying current with latest information



Meta Llama llama.meta.com

First Release: February 2023
Strengths: Open-source, customizable, strong performance
Best for: Custom applications, on-premise deployment, research
Considerations: Requires technical expertise; various sizes available (7B to 405B parameters)





Proper Attribution (research)
When artificial intelligence tools significantly contribute to your work, proper attribution is essential for maintaining transparency and ethical standards. Failing to acknowledge AI assistance where it played a substantial role can mislead audiences about the true nature of your work’s creation.
Example Attribution: “Initial drafts of this literature review were developed with assistance from Claude (Sonnet 4). All sources were independently verified, analysis was conducted by the author, and conclusions represent the author’s professional judgment.”
Do you require more thorough record-keeping? Use a documentation form instead
